Balanced can cause the first-message spike. With BIOS OS Controlled and C-states enabled, ESXi Balanced allows the CPU to enter deep C-states and drop to low P-states when idle. Mechanism and reason
ESXi memory accounting with Transparent Page Sharing:
* Consumed = physical memory actually backed by the host for the VM working set.
* Shared = pages that are identical across different VMs and therefore backed once.
* Shared common = pages identical within the same VM and therefore backed once.
* Balloon / Compressed / Swapped = 0 means the host has no memory pressure and is not reclaiming.

Net physical memory freed by sharing = ~755 GB – 713 GB ≈ 42 GB Consumed reduction.

* Inter-VM sharing now accounts for ~64 GB of pages that would otherwise be 64 GB × N copies.

In vSphere 8.0 and later SIOC is removed from the product. vSphere 9.1 has no Storage I/O Control setting per datastore and the feature cannot be turned on. Even in releases where SIOC existed it would not help this case: SIOC is a per-host, per-datastore throttling mechanism that arbitrates I/O between VMs running on the same ESXi host. It has no visibility across hosts and it cannot control the physical contention generated on the shared FC array by a VM running on host A versus a VM running on host B on the same VMFS datastore. The 1 ms -> 25 ms read latency rise you see on db-11 is array / shared-bus / queue contention caused by rpt-07’s large sequential reads on the same LUN, not hypervisor scheduling contention inside one host.

* Confirm the contention is outside the hypervisor. Check array metrics for that LUN / port group / FC queue depth during 01:00-03:00, and ESXi host `datastore latency`, `queue full`, `commands aborted` for the VMFS volume. VM level `Read latency` and `Kernel` latency on db-11 will separate storage from VM.
* Isolate the workload. Move rpt-07 or db-11 to a different datastore / LUN / storage pool, or schedule the reporting job to off-hours or throttle it at the VM level with a vSphere I/O Limit on rpt-07, CPU ready limits, or application-side throttling.
* Use array QoS / performance policies if the array supports it, e.g., limit IOPS / MB/s for the reporting VM’s LUN or give the DB LUN higher priority/service level.
* Avoid co-locating a noisy sequential scan VM with latency-sensitive DB VMs on the same physical spindle/SSD pool.

Conclusion: Balloon and Swapped are caused by the resource pool memory limit, not by host over-commit. Moving the VM or disabling balloon will not fix it, and will make it worse.

Mechanism and reason
The effective memory cap for rpt-app-03 is the RP-Reporting pool limit of 24,576 MB. Pool memory limit is enforced by the hypervisor across the pool, independent of host free memory.

Pool configured memory is 40 GB, but the pool’s active memory is constrained to ~24.3 GB consumed, which is essentially the 24.576 GB limit. With three VMs in the pool sharing that cap, the scheduler must reclaim memory inside the pool.

Granted ~15.4 GB for rpt-app-03 is below its 16 GB config and below its active need. The ~4.8 GB balloon and ~2.1 GB swap seen in vSphere metrics are the pool-level reclaim acting on the VM. The guest sees balloon memory disappear, so Linux uses its own swap: 3 GB guest swap in use, almost no free. Host is high because the pool is capped, not because the host is full. No balloon/swap outside the pool confirms the containment.

What to check next / what to change
The pool limit is the controlling constraint. Raising or removing the RP-Reporting memory limit, or increasing the reservation for the VMs that need it, will allow the pool to grant the memory the VMs actually need.

No. A high VM CPU Wait by itself does not mean the VM is stuck waiting on disk or memory.

VM CPU Wait includes idle time. From the vCPU scheduler view

Run + Ready + Co-stop + Wait = 100% per vCPU

Wait = Idle + Swap Wait + Other Wait

Idle is time the vCPU is scheduled but has nothing to run. The hypervisor cannot tell truly idle from guest OS IO-blocked, so idle is lumped into Wait. Most VMs do not run at 100%, so CPU Wait is naturally high.

Swap Wait is the vCPU waiting for a memory page from ESXi swap. Other Wait is blocked by something other than memory: disk IO, network IO, vMotion, snapshots, etc. Both Swap Wait and Other Wait are contention and should be included in sizing. Idle should be excluded.

Guest OS iowait is idle time with IO outstanding inside the guest. VM CPU Wait is a hypervisor metric and is not a 1:1 map to Guest OS iowait. Guest OS IO wait can appear as VM Run or as VM Wait.

With 90% Wait, check:
1. Run and Idle for the VirtualMachine. If Run is low, Idle + Other Wait ≈ 100% and the VM is idle, not waiting.
2. Break Wait into Swap Wait and Other Wait. If both are low and Idle is high, there is no wait problem.
3. Only if Other Wait or Swap Wait are sustained and Run is not low investigate further: breadth, snapshots, known bug KB 85393, and VM disk latency.

High Wait mostly means idle, not disk/memory contention.

VM CPU Usage is HT-aware and throughput based. With two vCPUs on the two threads of one core both running all the time, ESXi records the core gain as 1.25x. Each thread is therefore charged 62.5% of a full core. That is the VM vantage point: Usage = Used + work done by kernel on behalf of VM, and it includes frequency and Hyper-Threading efficiency. Run, the capacity metric, would be 100% per vCPU. Run measures time, not quality: Run + Ready + Co-stop + Wait = 100% per vCPU. Used also accounts for the shared core, so Used is lower than Run.

ESXi host vantage point for that core:
* Core Utilization = 100%. Core Utilization reports 100% when one thread of the core runs and also when both run. It is static-frequency and counts a core as busy.
* Thread Utilization = 100% per thread, 100% average for the core. Thread Utilization is the capacity reading with Hyper-Threading on.
* ESXi CPU Usage % = 100% for the core. Usage is based on Core Utilization adjusted for frequency and Hyper-Threading. With both threads busy ESXi sees the core as fully busy; Usage (MHz) reflects the HT benefit.

So the VM shows ~62.5% Usage because of the HT accounting, while the host sees the core fully busy. Check VM CPU Run for capacity; use Usage/Throughput for performance.

Adding a host will not clear the red state. The red is an *Invalid* cluster state, not an overcommitted / capacity shortage.

**Why the cluster is red**
Cluster state red means the resource pool tree is inconsistent: a parent’s fixed reservation is smaller than the sum of its children’s reservations.

* Prod is a Fixed pool under the cluster root with CPU reservation 100 GHz.
* Its two expandable children are
  * Prod-DB 70 GHz Expandable
  * Prod-App 45 GHz Expandable
  * 70 + 45 = 115 GHz > 100 GHz parent reservation

With Fixed reservation the admission check is only the pool’s own unreserved capacity. The tree is inconsistent at the Prod level even though the cluster has 480 GHz total capacity and CPU/memory usage is <40%.

Admission control checks reservations, never usage. A host at 10% usage can still refuse a VM if its capacity is already reserved. The red condition can be created at any level and adding capacity at the root does not repair it.

The red was created during last night’s failover: HA restarted VMs, then a change edited the CPU reservations of the resource pools while VMs were failing over. Changing a pool reservation while a VM is failing over can turn the cluster red because the failing-over VM is not charged to the pool until failover completes.

**Risk to running VMs**
Cluster state Invalid: Running VMs: Some may not get their reservations.
The VMs of the lost host were restarted by HA onto the remaining 5 hosts. With Prod children demanding 115 GHz against a fixed 100 GHz guarantee, the hypervisor cannot guarantee the 115 GHz to the Prod-DB/Prod-App subtree. Entitlement for VMs in those pools can be reduced under contention, and DRS/HA placement is restricted because reservations that fully commit a host/cluster stop migrations. The cluster is also red for HA if HA can no longer meet its failover capacity.

**Fix**
Fix the tree, not capacity:

Mechanism and reason:

Controls that exist for a VM network adapter:
* Network I/O Control v3 on a distributed switch. Per VM network adapter you can set shares, a reservation in Mb/s, and a limit in Mb/s or Gb/s. NetIOC controls transmit only, enforces the limit even when the vDS is not saturated, and shares/reservations are relative/absolute per physical NIC through the vDS. * The lower of the adapter-level NetIOC limit and the port-group shaping limit wins.

Guest OS metrics and VM metrics belong to different realms and do not map. The VM is the virtual motherboard; the Guest OS runs on it. ESXi sees a guest-physical page only when it is first touched via a second-level page-table fault. Freeing, reusing and caching inside the Guest OS are normal memory writes that never reach ESXi, so the hypervisor has no visibility into how Windows classifies pages as In Use / Modified / Cache / Free. See vsphere/technology/memory/concepts/guest-os-vs-vm-memory.

Windows “In Use” is utilization inside the Guest OS realm. VM Memory Consumed is the VMkernel’s capacity view: memory that has been touched and therefore remains mapped to the VM, even after the guest frees it. Consumed, Shared and Reservation have no equivalent in Windows. The table in vsphere/technology/memory/concepts/guest-os-vs-vm-memory lists the mismatch explicitly; Utilization In Use has no VM metric, and VM Swapped/Compressed has no Guest OS counterpart.

Mechanism: ESXi visibility = reads/writes by the Guest OS; it samples Active recently-used pages and records Consumed pages ever touched. Guest OS visibility = its own page classification and page file. The two layers manage memory independently and are sampled at different times with different roll-ups.

Result: patterns diverge. A guest can show high In Use while the VM is idle; e.g. an idle 16 GB Windows VM shows ~7.2 GB In Use while VM Active is 0 GB. Conversely, a guest that frees memory will not reduce Consumed. Size the Guest OS from Guest OS counters; reclaim/ capacity from VM counters. vsphere/architecture/vm-vs-guest-os

Conclusion
vSphere has no network latency counter. The VM network metrics are throughput, packets, broadcast/multicast counts and dropped packets; latency is missing. Mechanism and why latency can rise without dropped packets

No. “Storage is fine” from VM-level metrics does not rule out a Guest-OS storage delay.

VM disk latency and IOPS in vCenter start at the virtual disk, i.e. at the VMkernel/virtual-device layer. Guest OS Disk Queue Length is a Guest OS layer counter. For Windows it counts requests active below the partition manager – requests waiting in Storport / the adapter driver, in service at the virtual/physical device, or on the way back. It does not separate waiting from service.

The wait that is visible to the guest but invisible to the VM is the time spent in the Guest OS before the command reaches the virtual disk. Little’s Law: guest queue ≈ I/O rate × time per I/O.

The guest queue minus the requests that are at the virtual disk is the average number of requests that wait inside the Guest OS. Requests at the virtual disk ≈ IOPS × VM virtual-disk latency, i.e. VM outstanding IO.

Mechanism and reason
* New host: 1 NUMA node per socket = 32 cores, 512 GB. 20 vCPUs / 160 GB fits in one node. With >8 vCPUs vNUMA is active, so power-on builds a single vNUMA node. The guest sees one NUMA node.

* Old host: 1 NUMA node per socket = 12 cores, 192 GB. The VM is now wide: 20 vCPUs > 12 cores per node. The chart shows a limit in effect. Memory|Consumed is ~39.6 GB flat for 7 days while Memory|Granted hovers ~42.7 GB and Memory|Effective limit is 40.44 GB. That flat Consumed with Granted > Consumed is the classic limit signature described in swap-and-compression: a limit caps ESXi backing, so Consumed stays at the cap and the small gap above is VM overhead. Swapped and Compressed move in opposite directions because ESXi is re-using the same budget: when a guest page is requested, ESXi must make room under the limit, so it compresses or swaps out old pages; the pages later brought back swap in / decompress. Compressed and Swapped are mutually exclusive outputs of the same reclaim path, so one goes up while the other goes down.

The VM is not host-constrained: the ESXi host has >300 GB free and no other VM swaps/compresses, and VM Memory Contention is low, ~0.2-0.9%. Change the limit. Raise the VM’s memory limit or remove it so Effective limit matches the configured 64 GB, or size the reservation to the real working set. answer_text:
By vSphere’s own definition capacity is space, not speed.

* vSphere’s nominal total capacity = base frequency × cores. No Turbo, no Hyper-Threading.
  * ESXi 01 : 20 cores × 1.0 GHz = 20 GHz nominal
  * ESXi 02 : 10 cores × 2.0 GHz = 20 GHz nominal
  So by the GHz measure the two hosts are equal, 20 GHz each.

Capacity for placement is counted in physical threads where a vCPU can run. Speed is performance.

* ESXi 01 : 20 cores with HT on = 40 threads. Space capacity = 40 threads.
* ESXi 02 : 10 cores with HT on = 20 threads. Space capacity = 20 threads.

That is the “space” capacity used for sizing. The same nominal GHz is 20 GHz for both hosts, i.e. 20 GHz of vSphere nominal compute cycles per second, but the amount of vCPU space that can be placed is 40 threads on 01 and 20 threads on 02. The 01 host can hold twice as many vCPUs with no Ready, it will just run them ~2× slower than 02. Performance and capacity do not correlate.

If you must pick from the listed GHz/threads options the space view is:
ESXi 01 → E. 40 threads
ESXi 02 → E. 20 threads

Nominal GHz view is A. 20 GHz for both hosts.

answer_text:
Conclusion: Ballooned and Swapped are caused by the RP-Reporting memory limit, not by host memory pressure. The two requested changes will not fix the slow VM and will make it worse.

Mechanism and reason
* The host is in High state, ~40% consumed on a 512 GB host, so host free memory is far above the Soft/Hard balloon thresholds. Host pressure is absent.
* RP-Reporting has a cluster-wide memory limit of 24,576 MB with reservation 0 expandable. Pool Consumed is flat at ~24.3 GB, i.e. the limit is hit.
* A limit is not visible to the Guest OS. Under a memory limit the direct result is Compressed or Swapped when Consumed tries to grow beyond it; ballooning is not caused directly by a limit. With a pool limit, ESXi reclaims inside the pool to keep the pool’s Consumed ≤ limit, even though the host has free RAM. Ballooned pages are removed from Granted and the Guest OS still sees them as In Use.
* The VM shows Granted ~15.4 GB, Balloon ~4.8 GB, Swapped ~2.1 GB. The Guest OS reports 16 GB total, almost no free, and 3 GB guest swap in use because the balloon driver has been asked to reclaim pages. The balloon is past tense – it can stay >0 while pressure is gone.

Requested changes
* sched.mem.maxmemctl = 0 disables balloon inflation. The pool limit will still be enforced, so ESXi will compress/swap more instead of ballooning. Guest swap will grow and application latency will worsen.
* vMotion to a host with more free memory does not help. The pool limit is cluster-wide; the VM can be capped by load elsewhere in the pool on any host.

What to change / what to expect
Raise or remove the RP-Reporting memory limit to a value ≥ the pool’s actual demand, or right-size the pool contract. Do not use a VM limit. After the limit is lifted the pool can keep the memory its VMs have touched: Balloon Target will fall to 0, Ballooned will deflate as the Guest OS re-requests pages, Swapped/Compressed will drop, Guest free memory will recover and application slowness should ease.
